combinedRatio.title: Combined ratio
combinedRatio.content:
The combined ratio is (claims + expenses) ÷ premiums earned for the property & casualty reinsurance business. Below 100% means underwriting itself is profitable before any investment income; above 100% means premiums alone don't cover claims and costs.

For Munich Re: 73.5% in FY2025 (down from 77.3% in FY2024) is a benign cat-loss year in a still-firm P&C reinsurance market -- well inside management's Ambition 2030 target of ≤90% through the cycle, and the main reason FY2025 net income and ROE both beat FY2024.

What to watch:

  • A jump toward or above 100% after a major nat-cat year (hurricanes, earthquakes) -- normal for one year, a problem if persistent
  • Reinsurance pricing: renewal volumes down double digits at several 2026 treaty dates signal a softening cycle that will eventually pressure this ratio back up
  • P&C only -- it says nothing about the life/health or ERGO primary-insurance segments

technicalInvestment.title: Technical result vs investment result
technicalInvestment.content:
The technical result is profit from underwriting (premiums less claims and expenses), before investment income. The investment result is income earned on the float -- premiums collected but not yet paid out as claims, invested in bonds, equities and real assets.

For Munich Re: both legs have grown together since FY2022 (technical result EUR4.0bn to EUR9.8bn FY2022-FY2025; investment result EUR4.9bn to EUR7.5bn) -- a reinsurer earning well from underwriting discipline AND its investment book simultaneously, which is unusual and part of why the stock re-rated. The DCF values the combined owner-earnings stream at cost of equity, not either leg separately.

What to watch:

  • Technical result falling while investment result rises -- would mean underwriting discipline is slipping and the portfolio is masking it
  • Investment result sensitivity to interest rates: a reinsurer's float return moves with the rate cycle, not with premium growth

premiums.title: Premiums / insurance revenue
premiums.content:
Gross premiums written (IFRS4, through FY2022) is total premium volume underwritten in the period, before reinsurance ceded. Insurance revenue (IFRS17, from FY2022) is a narrower earned-and-allocated figure -- premium recognised as risk coverage is provided, net of several technical adjustments.

For Munich Re: the IFRS4-to-IFRS17 switch at FY2022/FY2023 is an accounting break, not a business change -- do not read the level shift as a volume collapse. RevenueRestated in the data bridges FY2022 onto the new basis (EUR55.4bn) for YoY comparison; everything since FY2023 is reported as Insurance Revenue only.

What to watch:

  • Insurance revenue growth once past the transition, as the cleanest top-line read
  • Treaty renewal commentary (1 January, 1 April, 1 July dates) for forward volume and pricing, which this annual figure lags

roeRoi.title: Return on equity vs return on investment
roeRoi.content:
ROE is net income over average shareholders' equity -- the blended return across underwriting, investing and ERGO primary insurance. Return on investment is the yield on the investment portfolio alone (investment result over average assets under own management).

For Munich Re: ROE of 18.3% in FY2025 sits comfortably above the ≥17% Ambition 2030 target and well above the EUR cost of equity the DCF discounts at (~9%, see below) -- the core reason the DCF values the company on cash returned at that spread rather than on asset growth. Return on investment of 3.2% is only the float's own yield; it is ROE's smaller, steadier component, with underwriting (combined ratio) doing more of the work.

What to watch:

  • ROE sustained above cost of equity -- the spread the valuation is built on
  • Return on investment drifting with reinvestment yields as the bond portfolio rolls over
  • Both are FY-only here; Munich Re does not disclose annualised ROE/ROI at the half-year mark in this dataset

balanceSheet.title: Balance sheet
balanceSheet.content:
Shareholders' equity is assets less liabilities; plotted against total liabilities to show leverage.

For Munich Re (Münchener Rückversicherungs-Gesellschaft AG): equity that grows only through revaluations or share issues is not the same as retained earnings.

What to watch:

  • Liabilities growing faster than equity
  • Goodwill share of equity after acquisitions

cashDebt.title: Cash and debt
cashDebt.content:
Cash & equivalents against total borrowings (leases excluded unless noted).

For Munich Re (Münchener Rückversicherungs-Gesellschaft AG): the DCF's net-debt bridge uses these balances at the latest balance-sheet date.

What to watch:

  • Net debt trend versus EBITDA
  • Refinancing dates and covenants in the filings

epsDps.title: EPS and dividends
epsDps.content:
EPS is net income per share; DPS is the cash dividend paid per share (excludes buy-backs). Both are in major currency units.

For Munich Re: Ambition 2030 commits >80% of net result to dividends plus buy-backs, so DPS/EPS alone understates total payout -- the rest comes back as share repurchases, which is also why shares outstanding has fallen every year shown (136.0m FY2023 -> 127.0m H1 FY2026) even as book value per share rose only modestly. This is the mechanism behind the DCF's cash-returned-at-cost-of-equity valuation.

What to watch:

  • DPS growing in line with, not ahead of, EPS through the cycle
  • Falling share count as the other half of the payout, not visible in DPS alone

fcf.title: Free cash flow
fcf.content:
Reported FCF here is operating cash flow less capital expenditure -- for an insurer, operating cash flow is swelled by premium float movements, not a clean proxy for distributable earnings the way it is at an industrial company.

For Munich Re: the DCF deliberately does not value this company on FCF. It values cash actually returned to shareholders (dividends plus buy-backs, Ambition 2030 targets >80% of net result) discounted at the EUR cost of equity, with net debt held at zero because subordinated debt is already charged inside the net result used for the payout. Net income, not FCF, is the right anchor to compare against that payout.

What to watch:

  • Dividend plus buy-back cash versus net income -- the payout ratio the whole valuation rests on
  • Reported FCF swings driven by investment-portfolio turnover, which are not earnings signals

margins.title: Margins
margins.content:
Gross margin is revenue less cost of revenue; operating margin deducts operating expenses; net margin is after interest and tax.

For Munich Re (Münchener Rückversicherungs-Gesellschaft AG): the spread between gross and operating margin is the cost of running the business; a widening spread with flat gross margin means opex is growing faster than sales.

What to watch:

  • Direction of operating margin over several years, not one
  • One-offs (impairments, disposals) that distort net margin

ocfCapex.title: Operating cash flow and CapEx
ocfCapex.content:
Operating cash flow is cash generated by operations; CapEx is cash invested in fixed and intangible assets.

For Munich Re (Münchener Rückversicherungs-Gesellschaft AG): CapEx here is shown as stored (sign convention varies by ticker); the DCF splits it into stay-in-business and growth where disclosed.

What to watch:

  • CapEx rising faster than revenue
  • OCF that diverges from EBITDA

profit.title: Profit lines
profit.content:
Gross profit is revenue less cost of revenue; operating income deducts operating expenses; net income is after interest, tax and one-offs.

For Munich Re (Münchener Rückversicherungs-Gesellschaft AG): the three lines together show where margin is made and lost between the top line and the bottom.

What to watch:

  • Operating income growing slower than gross profit (opex creep)
  • Net income far from operating income (interest, tax, one-offs)

revenue.title: Revenue
revenue.content:
Revenue here is insurance revenue (premiums earned and allocated, IFRS17) plus the smaller non-insurance lines -- not a sales line in the conventional sense.

For Munich Re: reinsurance revenue is a weak growth signal by design -- the business targets profitable volume over the cycle (Ambition 2030), not revenue growth, so a flat or declining year (treaty renewals down double digits at several 2026 dates) can accompany rising profit if pricing and combined ratio hold up. Watch the Underwriting & Investment Result section instead for the metrics that actually drive this valuation.

What to watch:

  • The IFRS4->IFRS17 break at FY2022/FY2023 (see Premiums chart) before reading any YoY growth across it
  • Combined ratio and ROE as the better profitability signals than top-line growth
  • Interim rows show H1 seasonality (nat-cat exposure skews to H2 in some years)

sbc.title: Stock-based compensation and share count
sbc.content:
Stock-based comp is the expense of equity awards; shares outstanding shows the dilution it causes net of buybacks.

For Munich Re (Münchener Rückversicherungs-Gesellschaft AG): the DCF charges SBC as a cash cost and holds the share count flat, so this chart is the check on that assumption.

What to watch:

  • Share count rising while buybacks are advertised
  • SBC as a percentage of revenue
